title: The caliphate ends, 1924
hookLine: the Ottoman caliphate is abolished by the new Turkish Republic

lines: A PAINTER WITH AN ANCIENT TITLE.
cards: The new parliament of the Turkish Republic has voted, and an office no longer exists. That night in Istanbul, the man who held it is told he must leave the country.

He paints and plays music, and his title, as tradition tells it, reaches back to the first generation after the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. Before dawn he and his family are taken to a train west, into Europe.
He will not come back. In India, Egypt and Indonesia, Muslims read the news. Some weep.
Some shrug. Some start organizing to bring it back. Today: the caliphate ends.

teach.b: Start with the word. Caliph comes from the Arabic khalifa, a successor or deputy. After the Prophet's death, Sunni Muslims hold, the community chose Abu Bakr as successor; Shia Muslims hold that the Prophet had named Ali.
The title passed down, through dynasties and quarrels, until it rested with the Ottoman sultans. The same root reaches back into the Qur'an.
In Pickthall's words, when God tells the angels about Adam: "Lo! I am about to place a viceroy in the earth." A khalifa.
How much real power the caliph held changed a great deal: sometimes an empire, sometimes mostly a symbol.

After the Ottoman Empire fell apart following the First World War, the new parliament in Ankara first ended the sultanate, kept a caliph without a throne for a short while, and then, once the Republic was declared, abolished the office entirely.
The last caliph, Abdulmecid, went into exile.
How did Muslims take it? Not in one way. In India, a movement that had campaigned hard to protect the caliphate lost its cause overnight.
Some scholars gathered to talk about naming a new caliph, and nothing came of it. Others said a Muslim's faith had never depended on one office in Istanbul.
Today Muslims still differ: some hope to see a caliphate again, others organize their religious life through mosques, scholars and councils, and they argue about it openly.

teach.h: THOU WITHDRAWEST SOVEREIGNTY FROM WHOM THOU WILT.
teach.b: The Qur'an says of power, in Pickthall's words: "Thou givest sovereignty unto whom Thou wilt, and Thou withdrawest sovereignty from whom Thou wilt." An institution ends. Prayer goes on.

how: Muslims today organize religious life through mosques, scholars, councils and national religious bodies, and they hold differing views about whether and how a caliphate should exist.

games.q: you're the last caliph. the parliament has voted your office out of existence and you're told to leave before dawn. what do you do?
o: call on Muslims abroad to rise up for you.
board the train west with your family.
games.why: Abdulmecid and his family were taken to a train heading into Europe. he never came back.

practice: Bring to mind one institution you once counted on that has changed or disappeared: a school, a shop that held your street together, a family tradition.
Notice what it held for people, and who picked up that work when it was gone, if anyone did. If you pray, hold Qur'an 3:26 in mind, that sovereignty is given and withdrawn.

wordCard.voice: Khalifa. The title of the caliph, successor to the Prophet, whose office the new Turkish Republic abolished in nineteen twenty-four, sending the last caliph into exile. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a successor or deputy; the title of the caliph, and the word in Qur'an 2:30.

carryVoice: Your line: an institution ends. Offices pass; the questions they raise stay. See you tomorrow.
